text: A cyclist increases speed uniformly from 4 m/s to 10 m/s in 2 seconds. Find the cyclist's acceleration.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: The cyclist's speed changes uniformly over a known time interval, so the standard acceleration relation applies.
Select a = (v − u)/t.
Substitute v = 10 m/s, u = 4 m/s, t = 2 s: a = (10 − 4)/2.
Compute a = 6/2 = 3 m/s².

5 m/s².misconception: forgot to subtract the initial velocity, using a = v/t = 10/2 instead

7 m/s².misconception: added the velocities instead of subtracting them, (10 + 4)/2

1.5 m/s².misconception: arithmetic slip, halving the correct answer by mistake

text: A stone is dropped from rest and falls freely under gravity (g = 10 m/s²). If it covers 35 m during the 4th second of its fall, find the total height fallen in those 4 seconds.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: This uses the 'distance in the nth second' relation for free fall from rest, combined with the total-distance formula.
Select s_n = (g/2)(2n − 1) to find the number of seconds n, then h = ½gt² for the total height.
Substitute s_n = 35, g = 10: 35 = 5(2n − 1), so 2n − 1 = 7, giving n = 4 s. Then h = ½ × 10 × 4².
Compute h = ½ × 10 × 16 = 80 m.

140 m.misconception: assumed the stone falls the same 35 m in every second and simply multiplied by n = 4 instead of using the free-fall relations

160 m.misconception: correctly solved n = 4 s but then forgot the factor ½ in h = ½gt², using h = gt² instead

70 m.misconception: simply doubled the last-second distance (35×2) instead of computing the total height properly

text: A particle moving along a straight line has velocity v = (6t − 3t²) m/s, where t is in seconds. Find the total distance traveled by the particle during the first 3 seconds.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: The velocity changes sign within the interval (v = 0 at t = 0 and t = 2 s), so displacement and distance differ and the path must be split at the turning point.
solution_steps.concept_tested: identifying a direction reversal within the interval

solution_steps.step_text: Select x(t) = ∫v dt = 3t² − t³ to track position, then compute distance as the sum of |Δx| over each monotonic segment.
Substitute: x(0) = 0, x(2) = 3(4) − 8 = 4 m, x(3) = 3(9) − 27 = 0 m. Segment distances: |4 − 0| = 4 m and |0 − 4| = 4 m.
Compute total distance = 4 + 4 = 8 m.

0 m.misconception: computed only the net displacement x(3) − x(0), confusing displacement with distance and ignoring the direction reversal

4 m.misconception: only accounted for the forward phase (0 to 2 s) and forgot the backward phase after the particle reversed direction

12 m.misconception: triple-counted the forward-phase distance due to confusion about the reversal instead of correctly adding the two 4 m segments

text: A ball is thrown horizontally with a speed of 6 m/s from the top of a tower of height 45 m. Taking g = 10 m/s², find the horizontal distance from the base of the tower where the ball lands.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: The horizontal range depends on the time of fall, which is found from the vertical motion alone.
solution_steps.concept_tested: identifying independence of horizontal and vertical motion

solution_steps.step_text: Select t = √(2h/g) and range = v × t.
Substitute h = 45 m, g = 10 m/s²: t = √9 = 3 s. Then range = 6 × 3.
Compute range = 18 m.

54 m.misconception: forgot to take the square root when finding time, using t = 2h/g = 9 s directly

27 m.misconception: used t = h/g = 4.5 s, omitting the factor of 2 inside the square root formula

2 m.misconception: divided the horizontal speed by the time instead of multiplying

text: A projectile is launched with a speed of 25 m/s at an angle of 53° to the horizontal. Taking g = 10 m/s² and sin 53° = 0.8, find its time of flight.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: The time of flight depends only on the vertical component of the initial velocity.
Select T = 2u sinθ/g.
Compute T = 4 s.

2 s.misconception: forgot the factor of 2, using T = u sinθ/g instead of 2u sinθ/g

8 s.misconception: double-counted the factor of 2, using T = 4u sinθ/g instead of 2u sinθ/g

text: A net force of 15 N produces an acceleration of 3 m/s² in a body. Find the mass of the body.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: Newton's second law relates the net force, mass, and acceleration of the body.
Select m = F/a.
Substitute F = 15 N, a = 3 m/s²: m = 15/3.
Compute m = 5 kg.

45 kg.misconception: multiplied force and acceleration instead of dividing (15×3)

0.2 kg.misconception: inverted the formula, computing a/F instead of F/a

12 kg.misconception: subtracted acceleration from force (15 − 3) instead of dividing

text: A lift of mass 500 kg accelerates upward at 2 m/s². Taking g = 10 m/s², find the tension in the supporting cable.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: The cable must support the lift's weight and additionally provide the net force for its upward acceleration.
solution_steps.concept_tested: identifying the forces acting on the accelerating lift

solution_steps.step_text: Select T = m(g + a).
Substitute m = 500 kg, g = 10 m/s², a = 2 m/s²: T = 500 × 12.
Compute T = 6000 N.

5000 N.misconception: forgot the acceleration term entirely, using T = mg

1000 N.misconception: forgot the weight term entirely, using T = ma only

4000 N.misconception: sign error, used T = m(g − a) instead of T = m(g + a)

text: Two blocks of masses 3 kg and 2 kg are in contact on a frictionless horizontal surface. A horizontal force of 20 N is applied to the 3 kg block, pushing both blocks together. Find the contact force between the two blocks.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: Both blocks share a common acceleration, and the contact force is the only force acting on the second (2 kg) block.
solution_steps.concept_tested: identifying the two-block system and isolating the second block

solution_steps.step_text: Select a = F/(m1 + m2) for the system, then contact force N = m2 × a.
Substitute F = 20 N, m1 = 3 kg, m2 = 2 kg: a = 20/5 = 4 m/s². Then N = 2 × 4.
Compute N = 8 N.

20 N.misconception: assumed the entire applied force is directly transmitted as the contact force

12 N.misconception: used the 3 kg mass instead of the 2 kg mass in N = ma

4 N.misconception: reported the system's acceleration value directly instead of multiplying it by the 2 kg mass

text: A block of mass 10 kg rests on a horizontal surface with coefficient of static friction 0.4. Taking g = 10 m/s², find the minimum horizontal force needed to just start moving the block.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: The block begins to move once the applied force equals the maximum static friction force.
Select f = μmg.
Substitute μ = 0.4, m = 10 kg, g = 10 m/s²: f = 0.4×10×10.
Compute f = 40 N.

100 N.misconception: forgot to include μ, computing mg directly

4 N.misconception: forgot to include g, computing μm directly

25 N.misconception: divided mg by μ instead of multiplying by μ

text: A block of mass 10 kg is placed on a rough horizontal surface (μ = 0.25). A horizontal force of 30 N is applied. Taking g = 10 m/s², find the block's acceleration.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: The net force on the block is the applied force minus the opposing kinetic friction force.
Select f = μmg, and a = (F − f)/m.
Substitute μ = 0.25, m = 10 kg, g = 10 m/s²: f = 25 N. Net force = 30 − 25 = 5 N.
Compute a = 5/10 = 0.5 m/s².

3 m/s².misconception: ignored friction entirely, computing a = F/m

5 m/s².misconception: correctly found the net force but forgot to divide by the mass

5.5 m/s².misconception: sign error, added the friction force to the applied force instead of subtracting it

text: A body of mass 4 kg is moving with a speed of 5 m/s. Find its kinetic energy.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: The kinetic energy formula applies directly to a moving body.
Select KE = ½mv².
Substitute m = 4 kg, v = 5 m/s: KE = ½×4×25.
Compute KE = 50 J.

100 J.misconception: forgot the factor of ½, using KE = mv²

20 J.misconception: used momentum mv instead of kinetic energy ½mv²

text: A 1000 kg car moving at 20 m/s is brought to rest by its brakes over a distance of 50 m. Find the average braking force.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: The work done by the braking force equals the car's initial kinetic energy, which is entirely removed.
Select KE = ½mv², and F = KE/d.
Compute F = 4000 N.

8000 N.misconception: dropped the factor of ½ in KE, using KE = mv² = 400000

200000 N.misconception: found the kinetic energy correctly but forgot to divide by the distance

2000 N.misconception: arithmetic slip, dividing 200000 by 100 instead of 50

text: A block of mass 2 kg is projected up a frictionless incline of angle 30° with an initial speed of 10 m/s at the bottom. Taking g = 10 m/s², find the distance it travels up the incline before momentarily coming to rest.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: All the block's initial kinetic energy converts into gravitational potential energy as it rises along the incline.
solution_steps.concept_tested: identifying the energy conservation scenario on an incline

solution_steps.step_text: Select ½mv² = mg(d sinθ), so d = v²/(2g sinθ).
Compute d = 10 m.

5 m.misconception: forgot the sinθ factor, computing the vertical-height formula d = v²/(2g) directly as if the incline were vertical

20 m.misconception: used sin²θ (0.25) instead of sinθ (0.5) in the denominator

100 m.misconception: omitted g from the denominator entirely

text: A 2 kg ball moving at 3 m/s collides with a stationary 4 kg ball and both move together after the collision. Find their common velocity.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: This is a perfectly inelastic collision, so total momentum is conserved and the two balls move together afterward.
Select m1v1 = (m1 + m2)v.
Substitute m1 = 2 kg, v1 = 3 m/s, m2 = 4 kg: 2×3 = (2+4)v, so 6 = 6v.
Compute v = 1 m/s.

6 m/s.misconception: found the total momentum correctly but forgot to divide by the combined mass

3 m/s.misconception: assumed the moving ball's velocity is unchanged after the collision

1.5 m/s.misconception: divided the momentum by the wrong mass (4 kg) instead of the combined mass (6 kg)

text: A gun of mass 10 kg fires a bullet of mass 0.05 kg with a muzzle velocity of 200 m/s. Find the recoil velocity of the gun.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: The total momentum of the gun-bullet system is conserved and was zero before firing.
solution_steps.concept_tested: identifying conservation of momentum for the recoil system

solution_steps.step_text: Select m_bullet × v_bullet = m_gun × v_gun.
Substitute m_bullet = 0.05 kg, v_bullet = 200 m/s, m_gun = 10 kg: 0.05×200 = 10×v_gun, so 10 = 10×v_gun.
Compute v_gun = 1 m/s.

10 m/s.misconception: correctly computed the bullet's momentum (10 kg·m/s) but forgot to divide by the gun's mass

100 m/s.misconception: misplaced a decimal point, treating the bullet's mass as 5 kg instead of 0.05 kg

2 m/s.misconception: mistakenly used half the gun's mass (5 kg) in the denominator

text: A stone tied to a string moves in a circle of radius 0.5 m with a time period of 2 s. Find its speed.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: The stone covers one full circumference in one time period.
Select v = 2πr/T.
Substitute r = 0.5 m, T = 2 s: v = 2π×0.5/2.
Compute v = π/2 m/s.

π m/s.misconception: forgot to divide by the period, using 2πr directly as the speed

π/4 m/s.misconception: dropped the factor of 2 in the circumference formula, using πr instead of 2πr

0.5 m/s.misconception: omitted π entirely, treating the circumference as 2r instead of 2πr

text: A car of mass 1000 kg goes round a flat circular curve of radius 20 m. If the coefficient of friction between the tires and the road is 0.5, find the maximum speed at which the car can take the turn without skidding. Take g = 10 m/s².
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: On a flat curve, friction alone supplies the centripetal force needed to keep the car turning.
solution_steps.concept_tested: identifying friction as the source of centripetal force

solution_steps.step_text: Select v_max = √(μgr).
Compute v_max = 10 m/s.

100 m/s.misconception: forgot to take the square root, reporting μgr directly

20 m/s.misconception: doubled the correct speed, confusing the given radius with a diameter

5 m/s.misconception: halved the correct speed by the same radius-diameter confusion in the opposite direction

text: A car takes a turn on a frictionless banked road of radius 45 m, where the banking angle θ satisfies tanθ = 0.5. Taking g = 10 m/s², find the maximum safe speed of the car on this curve.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: On a frictionless banked curve, the horizontal component of the normal force alone supplies the centripetal force.
Select v = √(gr tanθ).
Compute v = 15 m/s.

225 m/s.misconception: forgot to take the square root of gr tanθ, reporting it directly

30 m/s.misconception: inverted the tangent, using cotθ = 2 instead of tanθ = 0.5

20 m/s.misconception: arithmetic slip while evaluating the square root of 225

text: A uniform rod of mass 3 kg and length 2 m rotates about an axis passing through its center, perpendicular to its length. Find its moment of inertia. (For a rod about its center, I = ML²/12.)
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: The rod is a standard rigid body with a known moment-of-inertia formula about its center.
Select I = ML²/12.
Substitute M = 3 kg, L = 2 m: I = 3×4/12.
Compute I = 12/12 = 1 kg·m².

3 kg·m².misconception: used I = ML², omitting the 1/12 factor entirely

0.5 kg·m².misconception: used L instead of L² in the formula

4 kg·m².misconception: used the about-the-end formula ML²/3 instead of the about-the-center formula ML²/12

text: A solid cylinder rolls without slipping down an incline of angle 37° (sin37° = 0.6), starting from rest. Taking g = 10 m/s², find its linear acceleration down the incline. (For a solid cylinder, I = ½MR².)
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: For a body rolling without slipping down an incline, both translational and rotational inertia resist the motion, reducing the acceleration below g sinθ.
solution_steps.concept_tested: identifying rolling motion on an incline

solution_steps.step_text: Select a = g sinθ/(1 + k²/R²), where k²/R² = ½ for a solid cylinder, giving a = (2/3)g sinθ.
Substitute g = 10 m/s², sinθ = 0.6: a = (2/3)×10×0.6.
Compute a = (2/3)×6 = 4 m/s².

6 m/s².misconception: ignored rotational inertia entirely, treating the cylinder as sliding without rolling, using a = g sinθ

3 m/s².misconception: used the hoop/ring rotational factor (1 + 1) instead of the solid cylinder factor (1 + ½)

text: A flywheel in the form of a uniform disc of mass 10 kg and radius 0.4 m rotates at an angular speed of 20 rad/s. Find its rotational kinetic energy. (For a disc, I = ½MR².)
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: A rotating disc's kinetic energy depends on its moment of inertia and angular speed.
Select I = ½MR² and KE = ½Iω².
Substitute M = 10 kg, R = 0.4 m: I = ½×10×0.16 = 0.8 kg·m². With ω = 20 rad/s: KE = ½×0.8×400.
Compute KE = 160 J.

320 J.misconception: dropped the factor ½ in KE = ½Iω², using KE = Iω² instead

8 J.misconception: forgot to square ω, using KE = ½Iω instead of ½Iω²

400 J.misconception: used R instead of R² when computing the moment of inertia

text: The acceleration due to gravity on the surface of a planet is 4 times that on Earth's surface, and the planet's radius is 2 times Earth's radius. Find the ratio of the planet's mass to Earth's mass.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: Surface gravity relates to a planet's mass and radius through g = GM/R².
solution_steps.concept_tested: identifying the relation between g, M, and R

solution_steps.step_text: Select M ∝ gR², so M_planet/M_earth = (g_planet/g_earth) × (R_planet/R_earth)².
Substitute g_planet/g_earth = 4 and R_planet/R_earth = 2: ratio = 4 × 2².
Compute ratio = 4 × 4 = 16.

8.misconception: forgot to square the radius ratio, using g_ratio × R_ratio (4×2) instead of g_ratio × R_ratio²

4.misconception: only considered the surface gravity ratio, ignoring the radius ratio entirely

32.misconception: mistakenly cubed the radius ratio instead of squaring it (4×2³)

text: A planet has mass 8 times that of Earth and radius 2 times that of Earth. If Earth's escape velocity is 11.2 km/s, find the escape velocity from the planet's surface.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: Escape velocity depends on both the planet's mass and radius, so a ratio comparison with Earth applies.
solution_steps.concept_tested: identifying the escape velocity dependence on mass and radius

solution_steps.step_text: Select v_e ∝ √(M/R), so v_planet/v_earth = √(M_ratio/R_ratio).
Substitute M_ratio = 8, R_ratio = 2: v_planet/v_earth = √(8/2) = √4 = 2. So v_planet = 2×11.2.
Compute v_planet = 22.4 km/s.

44.8 km/s.misconception: forgot to take the square root of the mass-to-radius ratio, using the ratio of 4 directly as the multiplier

11.2 km/s.misconception: ignored the differences in mass and radius, assuming the escape velocity is unchanged

89.6 km/s.misconception: used only the mass ratio of 8 directly, ignoring both the radius ratio and the square root

text: A simple pendulum has a length of 2.5 m. Taking g = 10 m/s², find its time period.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: A simple pendulum executes SHM whose period depends on its length and the local value of g.
Select T = 2π√(L/g).
Compute T = π s.

2π s.misconception: arithmetic slip, evaluating √0.25 as 1 instead of 0.5

π/2 s.misconception: forgot the factor of 2 in T = 2π√(L/g), using π√(L/g) instead

4π s.misconception: inverted the ratio inside the square root, using g/L instead of L/g

text: A block of mass 0.5 kg attached to a horizontal spring oscillates in simple harmonic motion with a time period of π/5 seconds. Find the spring constant.
subject: Physics

solution_steps.step_text: A spring-block system executes SHM whose period depends on the mass and the spring constant.
Select T = 2π√(m/k), rearranged to k = 4π²m/T².
Substitute m = 0.5 kg, T = π/5 s (so T² = π²/25): k = 4π²×0.5/(π²/25) = 2π²×25/π².
Compute k = 50 N/m.

25 N/m.misconception: dropped a factor of 2 in the formula, using k = 2π²m/T² instead of 4π²m/T²

100 N/m.misconception: introduced an extra factor of 2, using k = 8π²m/T² instead of 4π²m/T²

0.02 N/m.misconception: inverted the formula entirely, computing T²/(4π²m) instead of 4π²m/T²
